title: Take the error at face value, then check if it's actually true
explanation: `sudo queue-workerctl start` refuses with "already running (pid 31337)". Rather than assuming the control script is right, check whether that PID is real: `ps -p 31337` comes back empty, and `sudo kill -0 31337` (a no-op signal used purely to test whether a PID exists) fails with "No such process". The service genuinely isn't running -- the script's belief that it is comes from somewhere else.

title: Find where that belief comes from
explanation: `cat /var/run/queue-worker.pid` shows 31337 -- a pidfile left behind by the box's unclean, hard-powered-off shutdown last week. Reading the control script itself (`cat /usr/local/bin/queue-workerctl`) shows exactly why it's fooled: the `start` logic only checks that the pidfile *exists*, never whether the PID inside it is actually alive. A crash that leaves a stale pidfile behind will block every future start attempt forever, with no self-recovery.

title: Clear the stale state, then start normally
explanation: `sudo rm /var/run/queue-worker.pid && sudo queue-workerctl start` removes the false signal and lets the script proceed through its normal start path, which writes a fresh, accurate pidfile for the process it actually launches.

title: Verify the real process is up, not just that the script didn't complain
explanation: `pgrep -af queue-worker` should show the daemon actually running. The lesson generalizes past this one script: any "already running" check that trusts a pidfile's mere existence, rather than confirming the PID inside it is live (`kill -0`), will get fooled by exactly this kind of unclean shutdown.
